title: Six Crates, One Rope, No Second Try
audienceRationale: This child is a 9-year-old who scored 3/3 on unseen transfer while rating the experience 1/5 with confusion and hesitation flagged — the profile of a capable kid being bored and talked at, not a struggling one. The design therefore removes all question-answer framing: no equations shown, no per-loop amount stated, no confirm dialogs, no praise chatter. He is treated as the competent loader whose judgment the world depends on. Difficulty comes from genuine synthesis (all three targets collide inside one committed lever pull), stakes come from a real, finite, physical resource (rope strands), and respect comes from the absence of hand-holding. Child evidence is treated as uncertain observation, not preference — the design bets that low fun plus high accuracy meant under-challenge, and answers it with weight, consequence, and restraint rather than decoration.
openingPromise: A storm-cut canyon at dusk. A dark camp on the far side. One fraying rope line is the only way across, and the radio crackles: "Line's holding — barely. Load it right the first time." The child is the loader: the only person who decides what goes on that rope, and the rope physically tells the truth about the math.
firstThreeSeconds: Wind sound, a rope creaking taut across the screen, one strand visibly snapping loose with a twang before any words appear. The dock lamp flickers on over a pile of numbered crates. A single radio line fades in: "Camp needs 24 ration units. Six loops. Don't overload." A crate near the child's hand wobbles, inviting a grab. No menu, no tutorial card — the rope and the crates ARE the interface.
firstAction: Drag any crate from the dock pile toward the rope. The nearest empty sling loop opens like a hand and the crate settles in with a rope-stretch sound; the loop sags visibly by an amount proportional to the crate's number. This teaches the entire physics in one gesture: loops carry totals, totals have weight, and unequal loops will hang crooked.
interactionDemonstration: Stage one worked example: the radio says 24 units, six loops. The child recovers 4-per-loop mentally, drags a 3-crate and a 1-crate into loop one (it sags to depth-4), a single 4-crate into loop two (identical sag — visual confirmation without numbers), continues until six loops hang level, notices loop five sits slightly lower (he stacked 2+3), swaps the 3 for a 2, watches the line settle level, then pulls the lever with both the tension and the information to know he earned the send. Every judgment in that sequence was multiplication doing physical work.
coreInteraction: Drag numbered supply crates from a dock pile into sling loops hanging from a canyon rope; crates can be stacked so a loop's total is the sum of its crates. Each loop sags in proportion to its load, so the rope line itself is a live bar-graph of the child's grouping — equal loads make a level line, unequal loads make a visible tilt, but no numbers or equations are ever shown as totals. When the child believes the grouping is right, they pull a heavy lever with a full-arm drag gesture to commit and send the rope across. There is no confirm dialog and no arithmetic readout before commitment: the lever is the answer.
mathAsPower: Multiplication is the load-balancing physics of the rope. Recovering the missing factor (24 units across 6 loops means each loop must carry 4) is the only way to know what "level" means; constructing equal groups is literally the act of making the rope hang straight; interpreting the spoken supply order (and discarding canyon depth and waiting days) is the only source of the loop count in stage two; refusing to load surplus crates in stage three is the difference between a rope that carries and a rope that snaps. The world never states the equation — the child's multiplication reasoning is the only instrument that reads the rope correctly, and every send visibly succeeds or fails because of it.
stakes: The rope has a finite, visible strand count (five strands twisted together, shown up close at the anchor post). Every mis-send frays one strand with a loud fiber-snap and a whip of loose cord — the rope literally thins. The dark camp across the canyon is the human stake: silhouettes of tents with no light, a faint cold-wind sound from that side. If all strands are lost, the line falls into the canyon and the run ends there — the crossing failed tonight.
consequences: A wrong send is never a red X. The rope physically reacts: unequal loops make the line lurch mid-crossing, the heaviest loop tears loose, its crates tumble into the canyon with a long falling clatter, and one strand snaps at the anchor. Overloading in stage three makes the whole line shear at the midpoint. The crates that fell are gone for that attempt; the dock restocks with a fresh (regenerated, non-identical) crate set so the child cannot memorize a layout. The radio says only one short factual line — 'Line held sixty feet, then the third sling gave out' — locating the failure without explaining the arithmetic.
recovery: After a strand snaps, the rope re-tensions and the stage resets with a regenerated crate pile serving the same underlying structure (same targets, fresh numbers where the stage allows, fresh crate composition always). No hints, no shown equations, and no reduction in difficulty. The only scaffold is diegetic and earned: after two failures on the same stage, the radio adds one grounded observation — 'Third sling was hanging lower than the rest before you pulled' — pointing at the physical evidence of imbalance, never at the math. Strand count carries across stages, so recovery is real but the budget is shared.
progression: Stage 1 — Recover the hidden group size: Radio: 'Camp needs 24 ration units. Six loops.' Six empty loops hang; the dock holds crates valued 1, 2, 3, and 4 in mixed quantities. No per-loop amount is ever stated or displayed. The child must internally recover 24 ÷ 6 = 4 per loop and build six loops that each total 4 (a single 4-crate, or 3+1, or 2+2, or 1+1+2 — multiple valid constructions). The rope sags unevenly as a hint of imbalance but never shows numbers. Pull the lever to send.

Stage 2 — Extract the loop count from noise: The loops are shrouded in canyon fog — the child cannot count them. The radio speaks one order containing three numbers: 'The drop is ninety feet, they've waited five days — send 21 fuel cells, three cells to a sling.' The child must discard 90 and 5, deduce 21 ÷ 3 = 7 loops, and tap the fog to reveal exactly that many loops before loading. Revealing the wrong count and sending costs a strand. Then load 21 fuel-cell crates (values 1, 2, 3) so each of the 7 loops totals 3, and pull the lever.

Stage 3 — Leave the surplus behind: Radio: 'Eight medkits per loop, four loops. That's all the line will take.' The dock deliberately holds crates summing to 41 units — more than the 32 the order allows. The child must load four loops of exactly 8 (from crates valued 2, 3, 4, 5, 6) and leave the surplus crates sitting on the dock. Any attempt to cram extras 'to be safe' makes the rope groan louder with each added unit; sending an overloaded or unequal line snaps it. The correct send leaves visible crates behind on the dock as the rope carries the rest across — restraint is the final answer.
interactionContinuity: One interaction grammar across all three stages: drag crates to slings, read the rope's sag, pull the lever to commit. Stage two adds exactly one verb (tap fog to declare the loop count) that itself is a committed interpretation of the word problem; stage three adds no new verbs at all — its difficulty is refusing to use the existing verb on surplus crates. Strand count, dock, rope, and radio persist across stages so the three stages read as one crossing, not three levels. The lever means the same irreversible thing every time.
worldReaction: Every crate placed makes its loop sag by its value — the rope is a continuous, honest readout of the child's current grouping. Equal loads settle into a satisfying level line with a low harmonic hum along the rope; unequal loads leave a visible crooked profile and an uneasy creak from the heaviest loop. On a successful send, the pulley turns, the loaded line glides across the canyon in silhouette, and the far side reacts: stage one lights one lantern at the camp edge, stage two starts the generator (a distant chug and a warm glow spreading), stage three brings the full camp string-lights on across the canyon — the world brightens exactly as much as the math earned.
payoff: No badge, no confetti, no cheering voice. After the third successful send, the camera holds on the canyon as the camp lights come up window by window across the far side, the wind sound softens, and tiny figures move between the tents. The rope — however many strands it still has — hangs quiet and level in the foreground. The radio's last line: 'Lights are on. Good loading.' Then silence and the lit canyon. The reward is the world he changed and the rope he kept alive.
replayVariation: On replay, all three stages regenerate: stage one draws a new total/loop pair from a fresh-item pool (e.g., 30 units across 5 loops, 28 across 7) with new crate value sets ensuring multiple valid constructions; stage two authors a new spoken order with different distractor quantities (temperature, elevation, crew count) and a new hidden loop count; stage three regenerates a surplus pile with a different overage and different crate denominations, occasionally including a decoy where the surplus itself could form one 'extra loop' that must still be refused. Rope strand count can optionally start at four on replay for a self-chosen harder line. No item ever repeats verbatim.
visualDirection: Dusk canyon palette: deep indigo sky, burnt-orange horizon fading, cold slate rock walls. The rope is the hero object — thick twisted fibers rendered with visible individual strands, taut catenary curve, frayed ends lit by the single warm dock lamp. Crates are stenciled wooden boxes with large painted numerals and distinct silhouettes per value (fuel cells squat and metallic, medkits with a canvas strap). Loops are heavy canvas slings that deform under load. Fog in stage two is volumetric and tappable. The far camp reads as small, dark, and waiting. Lighting is the emotional meter: the child's side warm and lamplit, the far side cold until earned. No UI chrome except the strand counter woven into the anchor post itself.
motionDirection: Everything obeys weight. Crates have drag inertia and land in slings with a settle-bounce scaled to their value. Loops sag with spring physics; the whole rope line continuously solves its catenary so imbalance reads at a glance. The lever requires a long deliberate pull with resistance easing at the top — commitment should feel physical. Sends animate the line traveling in silhouette with parallax canyon layers. Failures are slow-motion for the first half-second (the lurch, the tearing sling) then real-time for the fall. Strand snaps whip with a fast curl of loose fiber. Camp lights fade up slowly, one source at a time, never all at once.
soundDirection: Foundation layer: canyon wind, rope creak keyed to current imbalance (more tilt, more creak — an audible math cue that never states a number). Interaction layer: wooden thunk and rope-stretch per placement, pitch subtly lower for heavier loops; the lever is a two-stage ratchet-and-release. Consequence layer: strand snaps are a sharp fiber twang followed by a whip-crack; falling crates get a long doppler clatter. Radio lines are short, compressed, and slightly distorted — one or two lines per stage, spoken once, replayable by tapping the radio. Success is quiet: pulley rhythm, then the distant generator chug and a warm low pad as lights come on. No fanfares, no sticker sounds.
usefulLibraries: matter-js (rope catenary, sling sag, and crate weight physics)
PixiJS (layered canyon rendering, fog, silhouette send animations)
GSAP (lever pull, slow-motion failure beats, light fade-up sequencing)
Howler.js (layered wind/creak/radio audio with imbalance-keyed creak intensity)
web-speech-or-prerecorded-VO pipeline for the short radio lines
engagementPrediction: Fun rating rises from 1/5 to ≥3/5, driven by tactile crate physics, the lever-commit tension, and visible world change; hesitation may persist (it is now productive deliberation before a costly commit, distinguishable from confusion because it precedes the lever, not the placements). Expected session length 4–8 minutes across three stages with 0–2 strand losses for this child given his transfer accuracy. Replay probability higher than baseline because regeneration plus the optional four-strand start gives a self-directed harder run; a non-replay with a completed run and mid-or-better fun rating still counts as engagement recovery.
falsifyingEvidence: The design's core bet is falsified if: (a) fun rating remains ≤2/5 with accuracy still high, indicating boredom was not the cause of low engagement; (b) the child fails stage one repeatedly at the missing-factor step (cannot recover group size without it being stated), indicating the Quest's isolated-target success did not survive collision and the synthesis claim was premature; (c) stage two errors concentrate on distractor quantities (loading 90 or 5 into the loop-count decision), showing word-problem interpretation collapses under synthesis load; (d) he crams surplus crates in stage three even after a snap, showing constraint interpretation is not transferring; (e) confusion signals appear during crate placement (not pre-lever deliberation), suggesting the diegetic no-equation format obscures rather than respects. Any of (b)–(d) is academic evidence against synthesis mastery; (a) and (e) are evidence against the engagement hypothesis.
